29298-the-bluff-of-the-hawk:
Anthony Gilmore wrote this Hawk Carse adventure, published in Astounding Stories in May 1932. Hawk Carse, the story says, was a creator of new space frontiers and a pioneer of vast territories for commerce. He shaped history through a long feud with Ku Sui, a powerful Eurasian scientist. Without the historian John Sewell, Carse might have passed into oblivion like other forgotten spacemen.

Sewell's Space-Frontiers of the Last Century remains the standard work, but it compresses many episodes. Gilmore tells one of them: a bluff, a trick, or a trap, as Carse faces Ku Sui's schemes. Readers get a pulp space adventure about reputation, cunning, and a hero famed for tricks that his enemies cannot quite see through.
3294-the-sea-hawk:
Raphael Sabatini builds this adventure around Sir Oliver Tressilian of Cornwall. Part one follows the huckster, Rosamund, the forge, and the intervener, through the buckler, Jasper Leigh, and a trepanning, to the Spaniard who seals his fate. Betrayed and sold into slavery, Oliver vanishes from England and returns under another name.

Part two names him Sakr-el-Bahr, the hawk of the sea. The captive, the renegade, and the homeward bound lead to the raid, the lion of the faith, and the convert. Marzak-ben-Asad waits among his foes. Sabatini writes swashbuckling romance at its best: a gentleman turned corsair, seeking justice on the sea that wronged him.
34583-the-german-pioneers-a-tale-of-the-:
The German Pioneers is a historical novel by Frederick Spielhagen, translated from the German by Sternberg. Donohue, Henneberry published it at Chicago in 1891. Its subtitle calls it a tale of the Mohawk. The first chapter opens in New York harbour in April 1758. Unusual activity fills the quay despite two days of fog and rain. A large Dutch three-master rides at anchor in the roads. Dense groups watch it from the shore in the wet. Its passengers come ashore as skin covered skeletons, a bystander says.

They pass on their way to the state house to take an oath. Sternberg's translation carries a German novel of emigration to America. The Mohawk valley drew such German settlers in that century. A frontispiece shows a man speaking gently to a girl named Catherine. The tale joins the crossing to the frontier world beyond.
48591-motor-matt-s-promise-or-the-wreck-:
Motor Matt's Promise, or The Wreck of the Hawk, is number 14 of Motor Stories, the weekly of thrilling adventure motor fiction from Street and Smith of New York. The number is dated May 29, 1909, and priced at five cents; the weekly cost $2.50 per year by subscription. Sixteen chapters carry Matt from the levee to the conclusion.

Motor Matt, called Mile-a-minute Matt, is at home with every variety of motor, from bicycles to submarines. His chums are Carl Pretzel and Dick Ferral, and his double is Joe Dashington. A bag of diamonds and a daring plot fill the middle chapters.
55694-flash-evans-camera-news-hawk:
Flash Evans, Camera News Hawk is a boys' adventure novel by Frank Bell, published in New York by Cupples and Leon in 1940. Its companion volume is Flash Evans and the Darkroom Mystery. The frontispiece shows a terrific railway pile-up, car after car.

Twenty-five chapters run from Cracking Silk through a train wreck, a bridge out, and Doyle's treachery to a fade-out close. Flash has worked nine months as a photographer on a small-city newspaper. The first chapter finds him on a basketball court, flipping a last shot through the net. News photography gives the young hero his dangers and his clues. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
65601-the-trail-of-black-hawk:
The Trail of Black Hawk is a frontier tale by Paul Tomlinson. Appleton brought the book out in 1924. The rights date from 1915 in the Great Indian Chiefs series. Everett Tomlinson's frontier books head the volume. Contents run past twenty-six chapters of the Black Hawk War.

Black Hawk takes the trail, pursued, and a devastated home open it. A hidden retreat, a needed rest, and a new danger follow on. A narrow escape, an Indian legend, and in camp fill the middle. The flag of truce and the rout come at the twelfth chapter. The swallow, an invitation, and a scouting party carry the tale forward. The fight on the Pekatonika and Apple River fort crowd the late list. Joseph Hall speaks first, a frontier boy in Illinois of 1832. Illinois was very frontier in that year of the war, he notes.
76242-the-beloved-of-hathor-and-the-shri:
Florence Farr and Shakespear wrote these two plays on Egyptian themes, with all acting rights reserved. The first play's action takes place on the roof of the Temple of Hathor. The second is set in a cave of Mount Bakhua, home of metal-working fire magicians near Sinai.

The authors ask that the plays be shown decoratively, not scenically, in their staging note. A simple white background or pale sienna hangings should frame the actors, they direct. Figures moving across that ground should recall ancient frescoes or illuminated pages, an aim in keeping with the ritual mood of both temple plays.
britannica-1911-hawk:
Hawk is a word of somewhat indefinite meaning. It often covers all diurnal birds of prey except vultures and eagles. A stricter use excludes buzzards, falcons, harriers and kites too. Even then over a hundred species remain. Their genera number from a dozen to above a score. Systematisers disagree on the count. Hawks generally have short wings and long legs. Their bills curve down directly from the cere.

The sexes differ greatly in size among hawks. Yellow irides deepen with age into orange or red. Young birds wear striped or mottled plumage below. Adults are generally barred, old males often plain beneath. The goshawk is the largest of the group. The smallest male is no bigger than a song-thrush. Hawks hunt boldly among trees, chiefly for birds. They wait patiently, then glide on the victim. Alfred Newton signed the account.
britannica-1911-mohawk: Mohawk is a short peoples entry in the 1911 Britannica. The Mohawk are a tribe of North American Indians. They were the chief folk of the Iroquois league. Their name may mean man eaters in that tongue. They call themselves the flint people in their own words. Their villages lay in the vale of the Mohawk river. Their land ran north to one river and south to hills. They met Dutch and English traders at an early date. They were the first Indians to gain firearms in trade.
podcast-joerogan-ZIcQwDkcaWk:
Researcher Lex Fridman visits Joe Rogan for episode 1422, an early meeting of the two hosts. Fridman would later become a major podcaster himself. He arrives in his trademark black suit and tie.

Rogan teases him about dressing so sharply for a casual show. Fridman calls the suit armor that helps him focus. From there the talk opens into science, machines, and big ideas. The episode is a good record of Fridman before fame, when his calm style and deep curiosity were already fully formed. That ease marks all of his later visits too.
podcast-tuckercarlson-eat9NlWfKwk:
Romanian politician Calin Georgescu tells Tucker Carlson that Antony Blinken and Emmanuel Macron killed Romanian democracy. Georgescu won the first round of Romania's presidential vote before courts annulled the result and barred him. He presents himself as a banned opposition leader robbed of an election.

Georgescu lays out his charge that Western officials pushed Romania to cancel the people's choice. He describes the legal moves used against his campaign. Carlson asks what the case means for democracy across Europe. Concerned and freedom-minded viewers get a stolen-vote claim from the man at its center.
the-sea-hawk: Raphael Sabatini's The Sea-Hawk is laid out in its contents under two part titles. Part one is named for Sir Oliver Tressilian. Part two is headed Sakr-el-Bahr. The pages shown give that contents list and the first line of a note. No chapter text follows, so the story itself is not shown. Part one promises Rosamund, a forge, and a Spaniard. Part two promises a captive, a renegade, and a slave-market. A judgment closes the list.
